spans.note: document title and Executive Summary heading, with blank lines

spans.assertion: the analysis used a dataset of 146,028 player-referee dyads from European soccer leagues, 2012-2013 season
the primary analysis compared players with very light skin tone (0-0.25) to those with dark skin tone (0.5-1.0)
the analysis adjusted for covariates including exposure, position, league, player characteristics, and referee country bias measures
the point estimate for the primary comparison is a 0.152 percentage point positive association (95% CI -0.077 to 0.382)
the hypothesis is not supported because the difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.193) at α = 0.05
the confidence interval includes zero, so the evidence is deemed inconclusive

spans.note: lead-in label for nuance bullet list

spans.assertion: treating skin tone as continuous rather than dichotomous produces a statistically significant effect (0.294 pp per unit, p = 0.045)
Germany shows a significant positive effect (0.690 pp, p < 0.001)
France shows a negative trend in the effect
the observed effect is substantively small, roughly an 8-12% relative increase from a baseline of ~1.2%
a power analysis found the study could detect effects of 0.25 pp with 80% power, and the observed unadjusted difference (0.097 pp) falls below that threshold
the adjusted risk difference estimate is 0.152 percentage points (95% CI [-0.077, 0.382], p = 0.1933), not significant at α = 0.05
after adjusting for games, position, league, height, weight, and referee bias measures, dark-skinned players have a 0.152 pp higher probability of receiving a red card than light-skinned players
this difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional significance levels
the confidence interval indicates the true effect could range from a 0.077 pp decrease to a 0.382 pp increase
the adjusted odds ratio estimate is 1.125 (95% CI [0.933, 1.356], p = 0.2180)
odds of a red card are 1.125 times (12.5%) higher for dark-skinned players than light-skinned players, adjusting for the same covariates
the odds ratio is not statistically significant, with the CI including the null value of 1.0

spans.note: section heading: Model and Estimation Details

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis is player-referee dyads, each a unique player-referee pairing during the 2012-2013 season
the outcome variable is whether any red card was given across all games in that dyad
the original dataset contained 146,028 dyads
124,621 dyads (85.3%) had skin tone data
after excluding medium skin tones, the primary (light vs dark) analysis sample comprised 110,023 dyads
after complete case analysis, the final analytical sample was 101,718 dyads
the light skin (0-0.25) group comprised 83,582 dyads (82.2%)
the dark skin (0.5-1.0) group comprised 18,136 dyads (17.8%)
a total of 1,254 red cards were observed
the overall red card rate was 1.233%
21,407 observations (14.7% of the original dataset) were excluded for lacking skin tone ratings from both raters
14,598 observations with medium skin tone (0.25-0.5) were excluded from the primary analysis to create a clear light/dark contrast
8,305 observations (7.5% of the eligible sample) were excluded for missing data on position, height, weight, or referee bias measures
two independent raters, blind to the research question, coded players' skin tone from profile photos
skin tone was originally coded on a 5-point scale from very light to very dark
the 5-point scale was rescaled to a continuous 0-1 scale
inter-rater reliability correlation was 0.923, described as excellent agreement
the two raters' scores were averaged to form the primary exposure measure
the averaged skin tone score was dichotomized into Light (0-0.25) and Dark (0.5-1.0) groups
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator of whether any red card was received in the dyad
the count of red cards (0, 1, 2) was collapsed into a binary variable due to rarity
98.8% of dyads had zero red cards

spans.note: subheading: Covariates Adjusted For, with blank line

spans.assertion: adjusted for player position across 12 categories
adjusted for player height (cm, continuous)
adjusted for player weight (kg, continuous)
adjusted for league country (England, France, Germany, Spain)
adjusted for the number of games in the dyad (continuous, mean 3.06, median 1)
adjusted for referee country implicit bias (meanIAT)
adjusted for referee country explicit bias (meanExp)
standard errors were clustered by player (1,242 clusters)
no weighting was applied; each dyad was weighted equally
the primary model used no fixed effects
the primary model relied on covariate adjustment instead of fixed effects
a sensitivity analysis used referee fixed effects (3,147 referees) to compare players within the same referee
the primary model was a Linear Probability Model regressing red card probability on dark skin, games, position, league, height, weight, IAT, and explicit bias
a secondary logistic regression model was fit using the same covariates
marginal effects from the logistic model were calculated to estimate risk differences on the probability scale
the hypothesis is not supported
the primary analysis provides inconclusive evidence, though the point estimate (0.152 pp) is positive
the result is not statistically significant (p = 0.193), so the true effect cannot be ruled out as zero
the effect is substantively small, about a 12% relative increase from the 1.2% baseline rate
the estimate is uncertain, with a CI spanning a 0.077 pp decrease to a 0.382 pp increase
the secondary odds-ratio analysis yields consistent results (OR = 1.125, 95% CI 0.933-1.356, p = 0.218)

spans.note: subheading: Important Qualifications and Context, with blank line

spans.assertion: point estimates across multiple model specifications are consistently positive (0.14-0.18 pp)
treating skin tone as continuous yields a statistically significant effect (0.294 pp per unit, p = 0.045)
Germany shows a strong, significant effect (0.690 pp, p < 0.001), suggesting geographic heterogeneity
referee implicit bias is significantly associated with red cards overall (p < 0.001)

spans.note: label: Reasons for null finding in primary analysis

spans.assertion: a post-hoc power analysis found the study could detect effects ≥0.25 pp with 80% power, and the observed unadjusted difference (0.097 pp) fell below this, suggesting underpower
red cards are rare events (1.2% of dyads), limiting precision
the effect varies substantially by league, potentially averaging out in the pooled analysis
dichotomizing skin tone may lose information compared to continuous measurement
the point estimate implies an absolute increase of 0.15 pp in red card probability for dark-skinned players (1.37% vs 1.22%)
the point estimate implies a 12% relative increase in red card rate for dark-skinned players
translated to game-level terms, this implies about 0.015 additional expected red cards over 10 referees, or roughly 1 extra red card per 67 referee encounters
the effect size is small but potentially meaningful given the consequences of red cards

subheading: Data Limitations, with blank line
general limitation of dyad-level aggregation, no specific new action named

spans.assertion: 14.7% of dyads lack skin tone ratings because no photos were available

spans.note: speculative caveat that missing-photo players may differ systematically

light-skinned players outnumber dark-skinned players 4.6:1

spans.note: general caveat that imbalance requires stronger adjustment assumptions

spans.note: caveat that lighting/photo quality may affect ratings
self-critique that dichotomization cutpoints are somewhat arbitrary

spans.assertion: raters were blind to the research question

spans.note: caveat that referee learning or player behavior changes cannot be distinguished
caveat that some dyads span multiple seasons with changing circumstances

caveat that referee-player matching may not be random

two-way clustering (by player and by referee) was not used

spans.note: caveat that games within dyads are not independent

spans.assertion: multiple model specifications and subgroup analyses were conducted
no adjustment for multiple comparisons was made

spans.note: caveat that this increases false-positive risk in sensitivity analyses
caveat about strong modeling assumptions in sparse cells

spans.assertion: data are from the 2012-2013 season only
the analysis is limited to four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain)
the sample includes male players only
the sample includes professional-level players only

spans.note: caveat that soccer-specific findings may not generalize to other sports
caveat about European cultural context differing from other regions
caveat that referee training and culture vary by country

spans.assertion: the model assumed a linear relationship between covariates and probability
the model can predict probabilities outside [0,1], though this did not occur in practice due to low prevalence
the model assumed no unmeasured confounding given the included covariates
this assumption is likely violated due to unmeasured player aggressiveness and game context
the analysis assumed missingness on covariates and skin tone ratings is random conditional on observed data

spans.note: caveat that MAR may not hold if photos are unavailable for certain player types

spans.assertion: the analysis assumed one player's treatment does not affect another player's outcome

spans.note: caveat this could be violated if referees adjust behavior after carding a player

spans.assertion: findings show reasonable robustness despite the limitations
results are directionally consistent across multiple model specifications
logistic regression and linear probability models produce similar results
results hold with referee fixed effects, though the p-value decreases to 0.15
the continuous skin-tone analysis supports a positive association
the primary limitation is statistical power for detecting small effects, not methodological flaws
the analysis uses appropriate methods (covariate adjustment, clustered SEs)
the null finding is credible given the small effect size and sample size constraints

spans.note: section heading: Final Assessment, with blank line

spans.assertion: this analysis of 101,718 dyads provides insufficient evidence that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players at α = 0.05
the adjusted risk difference of 0.15 pp, while positive and consistent across specifications, is not statistically distinguishable from zero (p = 0.19)
the evidence is not definitively negative but inconclusive
the point estimate suggests a small positive association
sensitivity analyses using continuous skin tone show a significant effect (p = 0.045)
Germany shows a substantial and significant effect (p < 0.001)
the null finding may reflect inadequate power rather than a true absence of bias

for publication, the finding would be reported as no statistically significant evidence of a red-card disparity (adjusted risk difference 0.15 pp, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.38, p = 0.19), noting the positive point estimate and cross-league heterogeneity warranting further investigation
